```julia
end
Base.iterate(c::Countdown3, k=c.n) = k <= 0 ? nothing : (k, k - 1)
Base.IteratorSize(::Type{Countdown3}) = Base.SizeUnknown()
Base.eltype(::Type{Countdown3}) = Int
collect(Countdown3(3)), sum(Countdown3(4))
```

```text
([3, 2, 1], 10)
```

With `SizeUnknown`, `collect` grows the output with `push!` instead of preallocating.

Define `eltype` in both cases. Without it, `collect(Countdown3(3))` returns a `Vector{Any}`, because the default `IteratorEltype` is `HasEltype()` with `eltype` falling back to `Any`. If the element type genuinely cannot be known from the iterator's type, declare `Base.IteratorEltype(::Type{Countdown3}) = Base.EltypeUnknown()` and `collect` will infer by widening, as it does for generators.

Also: `eachindex`-style reductions such as `sum` and `maximum` work with either trait, and `length(Countdown(3))` as written in your version was the only missing piece for `HasLength`.
What do the `IteratorSize` and `IteratorEltype` traits control, concretely? Why should I bother declaring them on an iterator type?

They tell generic code what it may assume about your iterator, and `collect`, `map`, comprehensions, `zip`, and reductions all read them.

`IteratorSize(::Type{T})`, one of:

- `HasLength()` (default): `length(itr)` must be defined. `collect` preallocates `length` elements. `zip` and `Iterators.take` propagate the length.
- `HasShape{N}()`: additionally `size(itr)` and `axes`; `collect` returns an `N`-dimensional array, and comprehensions preserve shape.
- `SizeUnknown()`: `collect` grows a vector with `push!`; `length` is not called.
- `IsInfinite()`: `collect` refuses with a `MethodError`; `length` is not defined.

`IteratorEltype(::Type{T})`, one of:

- `HasEltype()` (default): `eltype(T)` is authoritative. `collect` allocates `Vector{eltype(T)}` up front. If you leave `eltype` undefined, it is `Any`, and you get a `Vector{Any}`.
- `EltypeUnknown()`: `collect` starts from the inferred type of the first element and widens as needed; an empty iterator falls back to compiler inference of the producing function. This is what generators and `Iterators.map` use.

Consequences:

- Wrong `HasLength` without `length`: `collect` throws `MethodError: no method matching length(::T)`, while `for` loops work. Common first bug in a new iterator.
- `HasEltype` with `eltype` `Any`: everything downstream is `Vector{Any}`, and the slowdown shows up far from the iterator.
- `HasShape` lets `collect(Iterators.product(1:2, 'a':'c'))` return a `2×3 Matrix` instead of a flat vector.

A good default for a hand-written iterator: define `length` and `eltype` if you can (cheap and most informative); otherwise declare `SizeUnknown()` and either `eltype` or `EltypeUnknown()`. Never leave `HasLength` implicit when there is no `length`.
Why does `collect` of my generator give a `Vector{Union{Nothing, Int64}}` and `eltype` of the same generator say `Any`?

Because generators are `EltypeUnknown`: `eltype` on the generator object has nothing to report, so it returns `Any`, while `collect` discovers the type by running the function and widening as it goes.

```julia
f(x) = x > 2 ? x : nothing
gen = (f(x) for x in 1:4)
eltype(gen), Base.IteratorEltype(gen)
```

```text
(Any, Base.EltypeUnknown())
```

```julia
f(x) = x > 2 ? x : nothing
gen = (f(x) for x in 1:4)
c = collect(gen)
typeof(c), c
```

```text
(Vector{Union{Nothing, Int64}}, Union{Nothing, Int64}[nothing, nothing, 3, 4])
```

For an empty input `collect` cannot run anything, so it falls back to inference of `f`:

```julia
typeof(collect(f(x) for x in Int[]))
```

```text
Vector{Union{Nothing, Int64}}
```

The same mechanism governs `map`: `typeof(map(f, 1:4))` is `Vector{Union{Nothing, Int64}}`.

If you want to decide the element type instead of letting `collect` discover it:

```julia
typeof(collect(Float64, (x for x in 1:3)))
```

```text
Vector{Float64}
```

`collect(T, itr)` converts each element to `T` and fails fast if one does not convert; `Vector{T}(gen)` is the same idea. Use this at API boundaries where the element type is part of the contract. Do not use `eltype(gen)` to decide anything; for a generator it is never informative.
When does `lazy"..."` (a `LazyString`) actually help? My error paths are `cond || throw(ArgumentError("...$x..."))` and the string is only built on failure anyway.

In that exact shape it does not help: the interpolation sits in the untaken branch, so the happy path never builds it. Both versions allocate zero bytes when `cond` holds.

It helps when the message is constructed *unconditionally* and only sometimes used. The common case is a message passed as an argument to a checking helper:

```julia
require(cond, msg) = cond || throw(ArgumentError(msg))

f_eager(x) = (require(x > 0, "x must be positive, got $x"); x)
f_lazy(x)  = (require(x > 0, lazy"x must be positive, got $x"); x)
f_eager(3); f_lazy(3)
@allocated(f_eager(3)), @allocated(f_lazy(3))
```

```text
(208, 64)
```

The eager version formats the integer and concatenates on every call; the lazy version allocates a small `LazyString` holding the parts and formats only if someone prints it. `LazyString <: AbstractString`, so `ArgumentError(lazy"...")` and `showerror` work unchanged, and the message printed on failure is identical.

Other reasons to prefer `lazy"..."` in error paths, independent of allocation:

- Type inference. An interpolation with four or more pieces lowers to a `string(...)` call with an `Any` vararg; `lazy"..."` defers all of that past the call graph the compiler has to reason about. This matters for `--trim` builds and for keeping error paths from widening inferred types.
- `@assert cond "message $x"` is already lazy: the macro wraps the message so it is only evaluated on failure.

When not to bother: a message in a branch that is never taken on the hot path, or code where readability matters more than a few dozen bytes. Both are the normal case; `lazy"..."` is for helpers that take a message argument and for packages that care about inference of their error paths. It requires Julia 1.8.
How does lazy broadcasting work under the hood, and what does `@.` actually do?

A broadcast expression is first built as a lazy tree and then materialized in one loop. `a .+ b .* c` lowers to `Broadcast.materialize(Broadcast.broadcasted(+, a, Broadcast.broadcasted(*, b, c)))`:

```julia
a = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]; b = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]; c = [100.0, 200.0, 300.0]
bc = Broadcast.broadcasted(+, a, Broadcast.broadcasted(*, b, c))
typeof(bc).name.name, bc.f, length(bc.args)
```

```text
(:Broadcasted, +, 2)
```

```julia
a = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]; b = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]; c = [100.0, 200.0, 300.0]
bc = Broadcast.broadcasted(+, a, Broadcast.broadcasted(*, b, c))
Broadcast.materialize(bc)
```

```text
[1001.0, 4002.0, 9003.0]
```

Nothing is computed until `materialize`; the `Broadcasted` object is a description. That is why the whole expression runs as one fused loop with one output allocation, no matter how many dotted operators it contains. Fusion is syntactic: it happens for dots that appear in one expression, so two statements make two loops and two arrays.

`@.` adds a dot to every call and operator in the expression, and turns `=` into `.=`:

```julia
@macroexpand @. a + b * c
```

```text
(+).(a, (*).(b, c))
```

With an assignment, `@. z = a + b * c` becomes `z .= a .+ b .* c`, which calls `materialize!(z, bc)` and writes into `z` with no allocation at all.

Measured on 1.13.2 with three-element vectors:

- `y = a .+ b; z = y .* c` (two statements): two arrays, 160 bytes.
- `@. (a + b) * c`: one array, 80 bytes.
- `@. z = (a + b) * c` into an existing `z`: 0 bytes.

You can also consume a `Broadcasted` lazily without materializing: `sum(Broadcast.broadcasted(*, a, b))` computes a dot product with no temporary (verified: 140.0 for the vectors above). That is the mechanism packages like LazyArrays build on. For everyday code, fusion through `@.` and `.=` is what you want; `broadcasted`/`materialize` are for writing custom array types and broadcast styles.

Fix the allocations in this inner loop:

```julia
function update!(z, a, b, c)
    y = a .+ b
    z .= y .* c
    return z
end
```

`y = a .+ b` materializes a temporary array on every call. Fuse the two operations into one dotted expression so the whole thing becomes a single loop writing into `z`:

```julia
function update!(z, a, b, c)
    @. z = (a + b) * c
    return z
end

a = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]; b = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]; c = [100.0, 200.0, 300.0]; z = similar(a)
update!(z, a, b, c)
@allocated(update!(z, a, b, c)), z
```

```text
(0, [1001.0, 4002.0, 9003.0])
```

Broadcast fusion is syntactic: every dot inside one expression joins the same loop, but a dot in a separate statement starts a new one and allocates its result. The `.=` (or `@.` with `=`) directs the fused loop into `z` through `materialize!`, so there is no allocation at all.

If the intermediate `y` is needed on its own later, keep it, but preallocate once outside the loop and reuse it:

```julia
# partial
y .= a .+ b
z .= y .* c
```

Two loops, zero allocations per call. The general rule: in a hot loop, every `=` with a dotted right-hand side is an allocation; every `.=` is not.
`x[101:900]` copies, right? How do I slice without allocating, and what are the risks?

Yes, indexing with a range copies. `view` (or `@view`/`@views`) gives a `SubArray` that indexes the parent lazily:

```julia
x = collect(1.0:1000.0)
slice_copy(x) = sum(x[101:900])
slice_view(x) = sum(view(x, 101:900))
slice_copy(x); slice_view(x)
@allocated(slice_copy(x)), @allocated(slice_view(x))
```

```text
(6472, 0)
```

`@view x[101:900]` is the same as `view(x, 101:900)`; `@views` applied to a whole expression or block rewrites every slice inside it to a view:

```julia
@macroexpand @views x[1:3] .+ x[2:4]
```

```text
(Base.maybeview)(x, 1:3) .+ (Base.maybeview)(x, 2:4)
```

Risks, all consequences of the view sharing memory with its parent:

- Writes through the view mutate the parent: `w = @view x[1:3]; w .= 0` zeroes `x[1:3]`.
- Writes to the parent show up in the view, so a view is not a snapshot. If you need the old values, copy.
- Aliasing in kernels: `axpy!(view(x, 1:n), view(x, 2:n+1))` reads and writes overlapping memory. Base functions that assume distinct inputs may produce wrong answers.
- A view keeps the whole parent alive; a view of three elements from a 1 GB array pins the gigabyte.
- A view of a non-contiguous slice (`view(A, :, 1:2:n)`) is still a view, but it is not strided-contiguous, so it cannot be passed to BLAS or `ccall` expecting dense memory without a copy.

Prefer views for reading and for in-place updates of a sub-block; prefer copies when the slice outlives the parent, when the parent will change, or when you are about to hand it to code that assumes ownership.
How do I express "compute this value at most once, only if needed" in Julia? I don't want a dependency for a thunk type.

A zero-argument closure is a thunk; a `Ref` next to it is the memo. Fourteen lines, no dependency:

```julia
struct Lazy{F}
    f::F
    cache::Base.RefValue{Any}
    Lazy(f) = new{typeof(f)}(f, Ref{Any}())
end
function force(l::Lazy)
    isassigned(l.cache) || (l.cache[] = l.f())
    l.cache[]
end

calls = Ref(0)
lz = Lazy(() -> (calls[] += 1; sum(1:100)))
force(lz), force(lz), calls[]
```

```text
(5050, 5050, 1)
```

The closure runs once; the second `force` returns the cached value. `Ref{Any}` keeps it simple; if you know the result type, make the struct `Lazy{F,T}` with `cache::Base.RefValue{T}` so `force` is type-stable.

Base already covers the two most common instances of this pattern:

- A default that is expensive to compute: `get(() -> expensive(), dict, key)` and `get!(f, dict, key)` run `f` only on a miss.
- A process-wide value initialized on first use (Julia 1.12+):

```julia
getcfg = OncePerProcess{Dict{String,Int}}() do
    println("initializing")
    Dict("n" => 4)
end
getcfg()["n"], getcfg()["n"]
```

```text
initializing
(4, 4)
```

`OncePerProcess` is thread-safe and is the right replacement for a global `Ref` initialized in `__init__`. There are also `OncePerThread` and `OncePerTask`.

When a thunk is the wrong tool: if the value is always needed, compute it eagerly; laziness that always fires is complexity for nothing. And do not capture a variable that is later reassigned in the thunk; that boxes it (check `@code_warntype` for `Core.Box`).
I've switched all my `map`/`filter` to the `Iterators` versions because lazy is faster. Is there any reason not to?

Lazy is not faster; it avoids an allocation in exchange for recomputing on every traversal. If the result is used more than once, lazy does more work:

```julia
ncalls = Ref(0)
expensive(x) = (ncalls[] += 1; x^2)

lazy = Iterators.map(expensive, 1:5)
sum(lazy); maximum(lazy)
println("lazy used twice: ", ncalls[], " calls")

ncalls[] = 0
eager = map(expensive, 1:5)
sum(eager); maximum(eager)
println("eager used twice: ", ncalls[], " calls")
```

```text
lazy used twice: 10 calls
eager used twice: 5 calls
```

Other things the lazy forms give up:

- Random access and `length`: `Iterators.filter` has `SizeUnknown`; you cannot index it or ask how many elements passed.
- Element type: `eltype` of a lazy iterator is `Any`; `collect` recovers it by widening, but any API that reads `eltype` sees nothing useful.
- Multiple-collection `map(f, a, b)` and shape-preserving `map` over matrices have no lazy counterpart with the same semantics (`Iterators.map` over `zip` is the workaround).
- Debuggability: a `Vector` shows you the data; a nested `Generator{Filter{Generator{...}}}` shows a type.

Use lazy when the result is consumed exactly once by a reduction or another iterator, when the pipeline may stop early (`take`, `findfirst`, `any`), or when the materialized intermediate would be large. Use eager when the result is reused, indexed, returned, or small. Switching mechanically in either direction is a mistake; measure with `@allocated` and a call counter like the one above when it matters.
I'm getting `Vector{Any}` out of `collect` on my generator and everything downstream is slow. The generator is `(parse_row(r) for r in rows)`. How do I find out why?

`collect` on a generator infers the element type from `parse_row`'s results, so a `Vector{Any}` means `parse_row` itself returns `Any` for the element type of `rows`. Check that first, in a `julia_eval_code` call:

```julia
# partial
Base.return_types(parse_row, (eltype(rows),))
```

If it prints `Any[Any]`, the generator is innocent. Then narrow it down:

1. `julia_eval_code` with `using InteractiveUtils; @code_warntype parse_row(rows[1])` and look for `Any` on a local or on the return. Typical causes: a field of an untyped struct, a `Dict{String,Any}` lookup, a branch that returns different types (`nothing` on one path and a `String` on another is fine, two unrelated structs is not), or splitting a string and indexing the result without `parse`.

2. If `parse_row` is correct but `eltype(rows)` is `Any` (for example `rows` came from a `Vector{Any}` built by `push!` on `[]`), fix the container: build it with a typed literal or `collect` the source with a known type.

3. Once `Base.return_types` returns a concrete type or a small `Union`, `collect` will produce the matching vector with no further change to the generator. Re-run the `collect` through `julia_eval_code` and check `typeof` of the result.

If you need a typed result immediately as a stopgap while fixing the real cause, `collect(RowType, gen)` converts each element and throws on the first that does not fit, which is better than a silent `Vector{Any}`.
`return_types` gives `Any[Union{Nothing, Row}]`, and `rows` is a `Vector{String}`. But `collect` still gives `Vector{Any}`.

Then the widening is happening in `collect`, not in inference, which means some element at runtime is neither `nothing` nor a `Row`. Inference says what `parse_row` *can* return given a `String`; `collect` reports what it *did* return. The two disagree only if something returns a value inference did not see, which usually means a different method of `parse_row` ran, or `rows` is not the `Vector{String}` you think it is at the call site.

Check the actual values, in `julia_eval_code`:

```julia
# partial
ts = unique(typeof(parse_row(r)) for r in rows)
```

and `typeof(rows)` right where the generator is built. The common outcomes:

- `ts` contains a third type: there is another `parse_row` method (an older one left in the session, or one in another module) catching some rows; `methods(parse_row)` will show it. In a long-lived session, a stale method from before an edit is the usual culprit; `julia_kill_session` and recreate if `methods` shows a definition you deleted.
- `typeof(rows)` is `Vector{Any}` or `Vector{AbstractString}` at the call site because of how it was constructed upstream; the `String` you tested with was not what the generator saw.

Once the element types agree with inference, `collect` returns `Vector{Union{Nothing, Row}}`, and downstream code that branches on `isnothing` is type-stable.
Which is better, `sum(f.(v))` or `sum(f, v)`? They look equivalent.

`sum(f, v)` applies `f` while reducing and allocates nothing; `sum(f.(v))` materializes `f.(v)` as a full array first:

```julia
f_fused(v) = sum(abs2, v)
f_temp(v)  = sum(abs2.(v))
v = rand(1000)
f_fused(v); f_temp(v)
@allocated(f_fused(v)), @allocated(f_temp(v))
```

```text
(0, 8072)
```

Same answer, one extra 8 KB array per call for the broadcast version. In a hot loop that is a GC cost for nothing.

The pattern generalizes: `maximum(f, v)`, `minimum(f, v)`, `any(f, v)`, `all(f, v)`, `count(f, v)`, `mapreduce(f, op, v)`, `sum(f, v; init)`. Each takes the function as the first argument and fuses the map into the reduction. `mapreduce(f, op, v; init=x)` is the general form, and `sum(f, v)` is `mapreduce(f, +, v)` with pairwise summation for accuracy.

Where the broadcast form is right: when you need the mapped array for something else as well, or when `f` broadcasts over several arrays (`sum(a .* b)`, which has no `sum(f, a, b)` form; write `sum(prod, zip(a, b))` or `mapreduce(*, +, a, b)` instead, or use `dot`).

`sum(f(x) for x in v)` is a third option and also allocates nothing, but `sum(f, v)` is shorter and dispatches to specialized reductions for ranges and arrays.
Are `keys(d)`, `values(d)`, `eachrow(A)`, and `Iterators.reverse` copies or lazy?

All lazy. They wrap the original and are invalidated or changed if it mutates.

```julia
d = Dict(:a => 1)
typeof(keys(d)).name.name, typeof(values(d)).name.name, typeof(pairs(d))
```

```text
(:KeySet, :ValueIterator, Dict{Symbol, Int64})
```

`keys` and `values` are views over the dictionary; `pairs(d)` for a `Dict` is the dictionary itself. `collect(keys(d))` when you need an array, or `Set(keys(d))` for a snapshot you can test membership in after the dict changes.

```julia
A = reshape(1:6, 2, 3)
typeof(eachrow(A)).name.name, map(collect, eachcol(A)), typeof(eachcol(A)[2]).name.name
```

```text
(:Slices, [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]], :SubArray)
```

Since Julia 1.9 `eachrow`, `eachcol`, and `eachslice` return a `Slices` array whose elements are views, so `eachcol(A)[2]` is `view(A, :, 2)`; `collect(eachcol(A))` gives you a vector of those views, not copies, and writes through them change `A`.

```julia
collect(Iterators.reverse(zip(1:3, 4:6)))
```

```text
[(3, 6), (2, 5), (1, 4)]
```

`Iterators.reverse` is lazy and works for anything that implements reverse iteration (ranges, arrays, `zip`, `enumerate`, `pairs` of arrays); `reverse(v)` on an array returns a reversed copy. For a range `Iterators.reverse(1:3)` is just `3:-1:1`, a `StepRange`, so it is free.

The rule: anything named `each*`, anything in `Iterators`, and the dictionary accessors are lazy; the plain verbs (`reverse`, `collect`, `map`, `filter`) allocate. When a lazy object escapes a function, remember that it pins its parent in memory and reflects later mutation.

Why does this closure make my function type-unstable? The variable is a `Float64` the whole time.

```julia
function running(v)
    total = 0.0
    for x in v
        total += x
    end
    report = () -> total
    report
end
```

`total` is assigned more than once and captured by a closure, so the compiler stores it in a `Core.Box`, a mutable heap cell with an `Any`-typed slot. The closure reads `Any` from the box every time it runs:

```julia
using InteractiveUtils
function running(v)
    total = 0.0
    for x in v
        total += x
    end
    report = () -> total
    report
end
Base.return_types(running(Float64[]))
```

```text
Any[Any]
```

`@code_warntype running([1.0])` shows `total::Core.Box` in the locals. The box exists because the lowering pass decides captures syntactically: a captured variable with multiple assignments is boxed even if every assignment has the same type.

Fix: capture a fresh, single-assignment binding with `let`:

```julia
function running_let(v)
    total = 0.0
    for x in v
        total += x
    end
    report = let total = total
        () -> total
    end
    report
end
Base.return_types(running_let(Float64[]))
```

```text
Any[Float64]
```

Now the closure's field is a `Float64`, and `@code_warntype` shows no `Core.Box`.

Other equivalent fixes: compute `total` in a helper function and build the closure in the caller (`report = make_report(sum_of(v))`), or copy into a differently named variable (`final_total = total; () -> final_total`). The point is the same: the captured variable must be assigned exactly once.

Check for this whenever a closure is slow: the string `Core.Box` in `@code_warntype` output is the signature.

Fix this counter; profiling says every call allocates:

```julia
function counter()
    n = 0
    inc = () -> (n += 1)
    inc
end
```

`n` is reassigned inside the closure, so it must be shared mutable state, and the compiler implements that with a `Core.Box` whose slot is `Any`. Every `n += 1` unboxes, adds, and reboxes an `Int`:

```julia
function counter()
    n = 0
    inc = () -> (n += 1)
    inc
end
Base.return_types(counter())
```

```text
Any[Any]
```

Make the mutable cell explicit and typed with a `Ref`:

```julia
function counter_ref()
    n = Ref(0)
    inc = () -> (n[] += 1)
    inc
end
c = counter_ref()
c(); c(), Base.return_types(counter_ref())
```

```text
(2, Any[Int64])
```

`n` is now assigned once (it always refers to the same `Ref{Int}`), so it is captured directly as a field of type `Ref{Int}`, and the closure's return type is inferred as `Int64`. The `Ref` itself is one allocation when `counter_ref()` is called; the increments allocate nothing.

This is the general rule for closures that mutate captured state: do not reassign the captured variable; mutate an object it refers to (`Ref`, an array, a mutable struct). The `let` trick fixes captures that are *read* after reassignment; `Ref` fixes captures that are *written* by the closure.
Any captured variable that gets reassigned is boxed, so I rewrite every loop with a closure to avoid reassignment.

Not every reassignment boxes, and the test is cheap, so check before rewriting. On 1.13.2 (and on 1.10) this loop is *not* boxed even though `factor` is assigned twice:

```julia
using InteractiveUtils
function scale_all(vs, factor)
    out = similar(vs)
    for i in eachindex(vs)
        factor = factor * 1
        out[i] = map(x -> x * factor, vs[i])
    end
    out
end
s = sprint(code_warntype, scale_all, (Vector{Vector{Float64}}, Float64))
occursin("Core.Box", s), Base.return_types(scale_all, (Vector{Vector{Float64}}, Float64))
```

```text
(false, Any[Vector{Vector{Float64}}])
```

The closure is created after the assignment in the same iteration and does not outlive it, and the lowering pass handles that case. These do box:

- A closure created, then the variable reassigned afterwards (`x = 1; f = () -> x; x = 2`).
- A variable assigned in a loop and captured by a closure created after the loop (`total += x` in a loop, then `() -> total`).
- A closure that itself assigns the captured variable (`() -> (n += 1)`).

The analysis is syntactic and conservative, and it has improved across Julia versions, so reasoning from a remembered rule is unreliable in both directions. The reliable check is `occursin("Core.Box", sprint(code_warntype, f, argtypes))` or reading the `@code_warntype` output for `Core.Box`. Fix only the closures that show it, with `let` (for reads) or `Ref` (for writes), and leave the rest alone.
How does function composition work in Julia? What type does `f ∘ g` have?

`∘` builds a `ComposedFunction`, a struct holding the two functions; calling it applies the inner one first:

```julia
h = sqrt ∘ abs
typeof(h), h(-16.0), h.outer, h.inner
```

```text
(ComposedFunction{typeof(sqrt), typeof(abs)}, 4.0, sqrt, abs)
```

It is a plain callable struct, so it specializes like any closure, inlines, and can be stored in typed fields. Chains compose right to left, as in mathematics:

```julia
(sqrt ∘ abs ∘ -)(4.0), ∘(reverse, uppercase, string)("abc")
```

```text
(2.0, "CBA")
```

`∘(fs...)` composes a tuple of functions, handy when the pipeline is built at runtime (it needs at least one function; `∘()` is a `MethodError`, so handle the empty case with `identity` yourself).

Compared with alternatives:

- `x -> sqrt(abs(x))` is equivalent in speed and sometimes clearer when the arguments are not a single value. Use `∘` when the composed function is passed around as a value (`map(sqrt ∘ abs, v)`), not for one-off calls.
- `|>` is application, not composition: `x |> abs |> sqrt` computes a value right now; `sqrt ∘ abs` is a function you can call later.
- `ComposedFunction` has `.outer` and `.inner` fields and prints as `sqrt ∘ abs`, so it introspects better than an anonymous function.

Type `∘` in the REPL with `\circ` then Tab. The multi-argument `∘(fs...)` form requires Julia 1.4 and `ComposedFunction` as a public named type requires 1.6, so both are available on 1.10 LTS.
What are `Base.Fix1` and `Base.Fix2`, and why does `filter(>(3), v)` work?

They are partial application as named structs: `Fix1(f, a)` is `x -> f(a, x)`, `Fix2(f, b)` is `x -> f(x, b)`. The comparison operators have methods that return them, which is why `>(3)` is a function:

```julia
typeof(>(3)), typeof(==(2)), typeof(in([1, 2]))
```

```text
(Base.Fix2{typeof(>), Int64}, Base.Fix2{typeof(==), Int64}, Base.Fix2{typeof(in), Vector{Int64}})
```

```julia
filter(>(3), [1, 5, 2, 8]), map(Base.Fix2(^, 2), [1, 2, 3]), map(Base.Fix1(*, 2), [1, 2, 3])
```

```text
([5, 8], [1, 4, 9], [2, 4, 6])
```

Why prefer them to `x -> x > 3`:

- Every anonymous function is a distinct type, so `map(x -> x > 3, v)` compiles a fresh specialization each time the source line is evaluated anew. `Fix2{typeof(>), Int64}` is one type for every threshold, so code that builds predicates at runtime (`>(threshold)` in a loop) does not recompile.
- They print readably (`>(3)` rather than `#13#14`) and introspect: `(>(3)).x` is `3`, `.f` is `>`.
- They work as `Dict` values and struct fields with concrete types.

Since Julia 1.12 there is the general `Base.Fix{N}(f, x)`, fixing the `N`th positional argument; `Fix1` and `Fix2` are aliases for `Fix{1}` and `Fix{2}`:

```julia
clamp_lo0 = Base.Fix{2}(clamp, 0.0)     # (x, hi) -> clamp(x, 0.0, hi)
clamp_lo0(-1.5, 1.0), clamp_lo0(0.5, 1.0), clamp_lo0(7.0, 1.0)
```

```text
(0.0, 0.5, 1.0)
```

On 1.10 only `Fix1` and `Fix2` exist. For more than one fixed argument, or arguments in other positions on older Julia, a closure is the right tool; `Fix` is not meant to replace closures, only to name the common one-argument case.
`foldl`, `foldr`, `reduce`: when does the choice matter, and what is `init` for?

The choice matters when the operator is not associative, and `init` matters whenever the collection can be empty.

```julia
foldl(-, 1:4), foldr(-, 1:4), reduce(-, 1:4)
```

```text
(-8, -2, -8)
```

`foldl` is `((1-2)-3)-4`; `foldr` is `1-(2-(3-4))`. `reduce` makes no promise about order; it happened to match `foldl` here, but for a non-associative operator you must not rely on it, and for arrays `reduce` uses pairwise or blocked evaluation when it can (`sum` does, for accuracy). Structure-building operators show the difference most clearly:

```julia
foldl(=>, 1:4), foldr(=>, 1:4)
```

```text
(((1 => 2) => 3) => 4, 1 => (2 => (3 => 4)))
```

`init` is the starting accumulator. Without it, an empty collection has no value to return:

```julia
try
    reduce(+, Int[])
catch e
    println(first(split(sprint(showerror, e), '\n')))
end
reduce(+, Int[]; init=0), foldl(+, Int[]; init=0.0)
```

```text
ArgumentError: reducing over an empty collection is not allowed; consider supplying `init` to the reducer
(0, 0.0)
```

`init` also sets the accumulator's type: `foldl(+, Int[]; init=0.0)` is `0.0`, and `foldl(+, [1, 2]; init=0.0)` is `3.0`. Use `zero(T)` or `one(T)` of the element type, not a literal, when you want the result typed like the elements.

`mapreduce(f, op, itr; init)` fuses a map into any of these (`mapfoldl`, `mapfoldr` for the ordered versions). Guidelines:

- Associative and commutative operator (`+`, `max`, `min`, `*` on numbers, `vcat` on arrays): `reduce`, and let Julia pick the order. Prefer the named reductions (`sum`, `maximum`, `prod`) when one exists; they are specialized.
- Order matters: `foldl` (or `foldr`), which also compiles to a plain loop.
- Possibly empty: always pass `init`.

This concatenation is the slowest part of my program. Why, and what should I do?

```julia
function gather(vs)
    foldl(vcat, vs)
end
```

`foldl(vcat, vs)` copies the whole accumulator at every step: after `k` vectors it has copied `1 + 2 + ... + k` elements, which is quadratic in the number of vectors. `reduce(vcat, vs)` has a specialized method that measures the total length once and fills a single output array:

```julia
vs = [rand(Int, 10) for _ in 1:2000]
r1 = reduce(vcat, vs); r2 = foldl(vcat, vs)
r1 == r2
```

```text
true
```

Measured on 1.13.2 for those 2,000 vectors of 10 elements:

- `foldl(vcat, vs)`: about 160 MB allocated.
- `reduce(vcat, vs)`: about 176 KB allocated, i.e. the result plus small overhead.
- `vcat(vs...)`: about 838 KB; splatting 2,000 arguments costs more than the specialized reduce but is still linear.

So:

```julia
gather(vs) = reduce(vcat, vs)
```

Two caveats:

- The fast path is only hit for `reduce` *without* `init`. `reduce(vcat, vs; init=Int[])` fell back to the generic loop and allocated as much as `foldl` (about 160 MB). If `vs` may be empty, handle that case explicitly (`isempty(vs) ? eltype(vs)() : reduce(vcat, vs)`) rather than passing `init`.
- The same specialization exists for `hcat`: `reduce(hcat, vs)` builds a `Matrix` with one column per vector in one allocation.

For the general pattern of accumulating into a growing array, the alternative is to preallocate with `sizehint!` and `append!` in a loop, which is also linear. `foldl` with any operator that copies its left argument is the thing to avoid.
What exactly does a `do` block do? Is it special syntax for `map` and `open`?

It is general syntax: `f(args...) do x ... end` passes the block as an anonymous function in the *first* argument position of `f`. Any function whose first parameter is a function works with it.

```julia
r1 = map([1, 2, 3]) do x
    x^2
end
r2 = map(x -> x^2, [1, 2, 3])
r1 == r2
```

```text
true
```

`@macroexpand map([1]) do x; x + 1; end` shows the rewrite: `map(x -> x + 1, [1])` (plus a source-line annotation).

The idiom is most useful when the block is several lines, or when the function manages a resource around the callback:

```julia
path = tempname()
open(path, "w") do io
    println(io, "hello")
end
read(path, String)
```

```text
"hello\n"
```

`open(f, path, mode)` calls `f(io)` and closes the file even if `f` throws; the `do` form is the `try/finally` you did not have to write. The same pattern appears in `lock(f, lk)`, `cd(f, dir)`, `withenv(f, pairs...)`, `redirect_stdout(f, io)`, `mktempdir(f)`, `get!(f, dict, key)`, and your own functions: define `with_resource(f, args...)` to acquire, call `f`, and release in `finally`.

Two things it is not:

- Not a lambda with multiple arguments by default: `do x, y` destructures two arguments; `do (x, y)` destructures one tuple argument.
- Not deferred: the block runs when `f` calls it, which for `map` is immediately. Nothing about `do` is lazy.
Is there a cleaner way to write a function that ignores its arguments and returns a constant than `_ -> 0`?

`Returns(value)` (Julia 1.7+):

```julia
Returns(0)(1, 2, 3), map(Returns(:x), 1:3), typeof(Returns(0))
```

```text
(0, [:x, :x, :x], Returns{Int64})
```

It accepts any number of positional and keyword arguments and returns the stored value. Compared with `(args...) -> 0`:

- One type per value type (`Returns{Int64}`) instead of a new anonymous type at every source location, so generic code that stores or compares callbacks sees a stable type.
- It prints as `Returns(0)`, which helps when it ends up in a struct field or a `Dict`.
- It is a struct with a `value` field, so you can read the constant back.

Uses: a default callback (`on_error = Returns(nothing)`), filling with a constant through an interface that wants a function (`map(Returns(0.0), xs)`), a predicate that accepts everything (`filter(Returns(true), xs)`), and stubbing a function argument in tests.

Where it is not appropriate: when the "constant" is a mutable object you want freshly allocated each call. `Returns([])` returns the *same* vector every time; use `_ -> []` for that.
What is a "function barrier" and when do I need one?

A function barrier is a call from type-unstable code into a function whose arguments are concretely typed, so that everything inside the callee compiles to specialized code even though the caller could not.

```julia
using InteractiveUtils
function process_bad(raw::Vector{Any})
    s = 0.0
    for x in raw
        s += x^2          # x is Any: dynamic dispatch and boxing every iteration
    end
    s
end

kernel(data) = sum(x -> x^2, data)
function process(raw::Vector{Any})
    data = convert(Vector{Float64}, raw)   # instability ends here
    return kernel(data)                    # specialized on Vector{Float64}
end

raw = Any[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
process(raw), occursin("ANY", sprint(code_warntype, process_bad, (Vector{Any},))), occursin("ANY", sprint(code_warntype, process, (Vector{Any},)))
```

```text
(14.0, true, false)
```

(`code_warntype` writing to a plain `IO` prints non-concrete types in upper case, so `"ANY"` is the marker for an unstable local or return.)

`process_bad` does its arithmetic on `Any` values; `process` converts once and hands a `Vector{Float64}` to `kernel`, which is compiled for that type. The cost of the barrier is one dynamic dispatch at the call; the benefit is a fully typed loop.

When you need one:

- Data arrives untyped: parsed files, `Dict{String,Any}` configuration, `Any`-typed containers, results of `eval` or reflection.
- A branch chooses between types at runtime (`T = flag ? Float32 : Float64`); do the choice in the outer function and call `kernel(zeros(T, n))`, which specializes per `T`.
- Values come from a non-`const` global.

When you do not: if the caller is already type-stable, splitting it buys nothing. Check with `@code_warntype`: the barrier belongs at the exact point where types first become concrete. `Base.return_types` on the kernel should show a concrete type for the argument types the barrier produces.
Tuples and NamedTuples are immutable. How do I "update one field" without rebuilding by hand?

Use `Base.setindex` (no bang), `merge`, or splatting. Each returns a new object; the original is untouched.

```julia
nt = (a = 1, b = "x")
Base.setindex(nt, 2, :a), nt
```

```text
((a = 2, b = "x"), (a = 1, b = "x"))
```

```julia
nt = (a = 1, b = "x")
merge(nt, (b = "y", c = 3.0)), (; nt..., a = 10)    # replace b and add c; later keys win
```

```text
((a = 1, b = "y", c = 3.0), (a = 10, b = "x"))
```

```julia
t = (1, 2, 3)
Base.setindex(t, 99, 2), t
```

```text
((1, 99, 3), (1, 2, 3))
```

All of these are compile-time operations on the tuple type when the index or key is a constant, so there is no runtime cost beyond constructing the new tuple; for small tuples that is a register shuffle.

For immutable `struct`s there is no built-in field-replacing function; the options are a keyword constructor you write (`Point(p; x = p.x, y = p.y) = Point(x, y)`), or the Accessors.jl package (`@set p.x = 3.0`), which also handles nested updates and works on tuples and named tuples uniformly.

Trying to mutate fails fast, which is the point of immutability:

```julia
nt = (a = 1, b = "x")
try
    nt.a = 5
catch e
    println(sprint(showerror, e))
end
```

```text
setfield!: immutable struct of type NamedTuple cannot be changed
```

Prefer immutable values plus these update functions for small configuration-like data: no aliasing surprises, no defensive copies, and `===` comparisons work. Reach for `mutable struct` when the object is large and updated in a loop.
How do I update a field deep inside nested immutable structs without rebuilding every level by hand?

Use Accessors.jl. `@set` returns a copy with one (possibly nested) field replaced; `@reset` rebinds the variable to that copy:

```julia
# partial
using Accessors

struct Config
    name::String
    limits::NamedTuple{(:lo, :hi), Tuple{Float64, Float64}}
end

cfg  = Config("run", (lo = 0.0, hi = 1.0))
cfg2 = @set cfg.limits.hi = 2.0
cfg2                      # Config("run", (lo = 0.0, hi = 2.0))
cfg                       # Config("run", (lo = 0.0, hi = 1.0))  -- unchanged

@reset cfg.name = "run2"  # rebinds cfg; cfg.name is now "run2"

nt = (a = 1, b = (c = 2,))
@set nt.b.c = 5           # (a = 1, b = (c = 5,))
@modify(x -> x + 1, nt.b.c)   # (a = 1, b = (c = 3,))
```

(Verified with Accessors 0.1.45 on Julia 1.13.2.)

What it does: `@set cfg.limits.hi = 2.0` expands to nested `set` calls that construct a new `NamedTuple` and then a new `Config` with the constructor, passing the other fields through. For a `struct` with a default constructor that is all it needs; if you define an inner constructor with different arguments, define `Accessors.set` or `ConstructionBase.setproperties` for your type.

`@modify(f, obj.path)` applies a function instead of assigning a value, and `@optic _.a` names a path you can store and reuse (`set(nt, @optic(_.a), 10)`). Optics compose, so a lens into `_.limits.hi` can be passed to code that does not know the outer type.

Trade-offs: it is a dependency, and each `@set` allocates a new outer object (cheap for small immutable structs, as they are usually stack-allocated). For one flat `NamedTuple`, `Base.setindex(nt, v, :key)` or `merge` in Base is enough; Accessors earns its place when the nesting is more than one level or the path is data.
Does Julia do tail-call optimization? I wrote a recursive loop and it crashes on large inputs.

No. Julia does not guarantee tail-call elimination, so a recursion that is linear in the input size overflows the stack:

```julia
countdown(n) = iszero(n) ? 0 : countdown(n - 1)
countdown(1000)
```

```text
0
```

```julia
try
    countdown(10_000_000)
catch e
    typeof(e)
end
```

```text
StackOverflowError
```

The tail-recursive rewrite with an accumulator overflows just the same:

```julia
sumto(n, acc=0) = iszero(n) ? acc : sumto(n - 1, acc + n)
try
    sumto(10_000_000)
catch e
    typeof(e)
end
```

```text
StackOverflowError
```

LLVM may turn some self tail calls into jumps as an optimization, but nothing in the language promises it, and recursion through multiple functions or with non-trivial return types defeats it. Write the loop:

```julia
loopdown(n) = (while n > 0; n -= 1; end; n)
loopdown(10_000_000)
```

```text
0
```

Where recursion is right: tree-shaped problems whose depth is logarithmic or bounded by the structure (traversing an expression tree, divide-and-conquer on arrays, recursive descent over nested data). Depth there is tens or hundreds of frames, well within the default stack. Where it is wrong: anything whose depth grows linearly with the input (counting, list walking, iterating a sequence). For those, use a `while` or `for` loop, or manage an explicit stack with a `Vector`.

When a recursive algorithm is the natural expression and the depth may be large, convert to an explicit work-list: `push!` the pending subproblems onto a `Vector` and `pop!` in a loop. Same algorithm, heap-bounded instead of stack-bounded.
Does Julia specialize on function arguments? I see conflicting advice about `f::F where F` versus just `f`.

It specializes when the function argument is *called* in the method body, and does not when it is only passed on to another function. That is a deliberate heuristic to limit compilation; it also applies to `Type` and `Vararg` arguments. You can see it in the method's specializations:

```julia
apply_called(f, x) = f(x)                      # f is called here
apply_passed(f, x) = map(f, x)                 # f is only passed through
apply_passed_F(f::F, x) where {F} = map(f, x)  # type parameter forces specialization

apply_called(sin, 1.0);   apply_called(cos, 1.0)
apply_passed(sin, [1.0]); apply_passed(cos, [1.0])
apply_passed_F(sin, [1.0]); apply_passed_F(cos, [1.0])

for fn in (apply_called, apply_passed, apply_passed_F)
    println(fn, ": ", [mi.specTypes for mi in Base.specializations(only(methods(fn)))])
end
```

```text
apply_called: DataType[Tuple{typeof(apply_called), typeof(sin), Float64}, Tuple{typeof(apply_called), typeof(cos), Float64}]
apply_passed: DataType[Tuple{typeof(apply_passed), Function, Vector{Float64}}]
apply_passed_F: DataType[Tuple{typeof(apply_passed_F), typeof(sin), Vector{Float64}}, Tuple{typeof(apply_passed_F), typeof(cos), Vector{Float64}}]
```

`apply_passed` compiled once, for `Function`, and inside it `map(f, x)` is a dynamic call. Whether that matters depends on what the callee returns: `map` returns a concrete `Vector` either way, so the cost is one dispatch per call. For a reduction, the result type is lost:

```julia
using InteractiveUtils
sum_passed(f, x) = mapreduce(f, +, x)
sum_passed_F(f::F, x) where {F} = mapreduce(f, +, x)
code_typed(sum_passed, (Function, Vector{Float64}))[1].second, code_typed(sum_passed_F, (typeof(sin), Vector{Float64}))[1].second
```

```text
(Any, Float64)
```

The generic specialization returns `Any` and boxes the result; the `::F` version returns `Float64`.

Rules:

- A function argument that is only forwarded: write `f::F) where {F}` if the callee's return type matters to you or the call is hot. Same for `::Type{T}) where {T}`.
- A function argument that is called in the body: no annotation needed.
- `::Function` does *not* force specialization; see `Base.specializations` to verify in your own code. Nor does it help dispatch, and it rejects callable structs that are not `<: Function`.

`Base.specializations` exists on 1.10 as well, so this check works on LTS.
I annotate higher-order functions as `f::Function` so Julia compiles a specialized version for each function I pass. Is that correct?

No. `::Function` changes dispatch (it rejects non-`Function` callables) but has no effect on specialization. Julia's rule is about *use*, not annotation: a function argument that is only passed along is compiled once for the abstract type `Function`, annotated or not.

```julia
apply_fn(f::Function, x) = map(f, x)
apply_fn(sin, [1.0]); apply_fn(cos, [1.0])
[mi.specTypes for mi in Base.specializations(only(methods(apply_fn)))]
```

```text
DataType[Tuple{typeof(apply_fn), Function, Vector{Float64}}]
```

One specialization for two different functions. To force one per function, introduce a type parameter:

```julia
apply_F(f::F, x) where {F} = map(f, x)
apply_F(sin, [1.0]); apply_F(cos, [1.0])
length(Base.specializations(only(methods(apply_F))))
```

```text
2
```

Why the annotation is also a *restriction*: `Base.Fix2`, `ComposedFunction`, and `Returns` are `Function` subtypes, but a user's callable struct (`struct Scale; k::Float64; end; (s::Scale)(x) = s.k * x`) is not. `f::Function` rejects it with a `MethodError` for no gain. Leave the argument unannotated, or use `::F where {F}` when you need the specialization.

When *not* to force specialization: a function that is called once with many different callbacks (a registry, a plotting API) can pay more in compile time than it saves. Base's heuristic exists for that reason; override it deliberately, in hot paths, after checking `Base.specializations` or `@code_warntype`.
Design an API for registering callbacks `on_event(f)` that are later called in a hot loop. What should the storage and call path look like?

Separate the two costs: registration can be dynamic; the hot loop must not be.

Storage. A `Vector{Function}` or a field `callback::Function` is abstract: each call is a dynamic dispatch and the return value is boxed. Options, in increasing order of commitment:

1. Parametric struct per callback: `struct Handler{F}; f::F; end`. One handler is fully typed; a `Vector{Handler}` of mixed `F` is abstract again.
2. A tuple of handlers: `handlers = (h1, h2, h3)`. Fully typed, iteration unrolls, but the set is fixed when the tuple is built. Good for a pipeline configured once at startup.
3. Erase the return type deliberately: `Vector{FunctionWrappers.FunctionWrapper{Nothing, Tuple{Event}}}` (FunctionWrappers.jl) gives a concrete element type with a fixed signature, so the loop calls through a function pointer with no boxing. Right when callbacks are added and removed at runtime.

Call path. Whichever storage you choose, the loop body must know the signature. If the callbacks return values you use, fix the return type (`FunctionWrapper{Float64, ...}`, or document `Nothing`). If they only produce effects, return `nothing` and ignore the value; a boxed `nothing` costs nothing.

Default callback: `Returns(nothing)` instead of `identity` or an empty closure; it has a stable type and prints clearly.

Registration function:

```julia
# partial
on_event!(reg, f) = (push!(reg.handlers, FunctionWrapper{Nothing, Tuple{Event}}(f)); reg)
```

Accept any callable (no `::Function` annotation) so users can pass `Base.Fix2`, `Returns`, or their own structs.

What not to do: `Vector{Any}` of closures; `f::Function` fields; `eval` to generate a specialized loop per registration. And measure before adopting option 3: if events arrive at kilohertz rather than megahertz, the dynamic dispatch of option 1 with a `Vector{Any}` is already cheap enough, and the simpler code wins.
How do I map a function over pairs from `zip` when the function takes two arguments, not a tuple?

Use `splat` (Julia 1.9+), which turns `f` into a function of one tuple argument:

```julia
map(splat(+), zip(1:3, 10:10:30)), typeof(splat(+))
```

```text
([11, 22, 33], Base.Splat{typeof(+)})
```

`splat(f)(args)` is `f(args...)`; it is a named struct, so it specializes and prints readably. The equivalent closure is `((a, b),) -> a + b`, with the extra parentheses and trailing comma that destructure a single tuple argument, which is easy to get wrong.

Often you do not need `zip` at all: `map(+, 1:3, 10:10:30)` maps over several collections directly and stops at the shortest. `splat` is for the cases where you already have an iterator of tuples (`zip` inside a longer pipeline, `Iterators.product`, a `Vector{Tuple}` from a parser, `pairs`).

On 1.10 `splat` exists and is exported as well (it was added in 1.9; the struct is `Base.Splat` there too). Before 1.9 the same thing was `Base.splat`, unexported.
Are closures and anonymous functions just function pointers in Julia?

No. Each one is a struct type generated by the compiler. The captured variables are its fields, and the function body is a method on that type.

```julia
mk(a) = x -> a * x
cl = mk(3)
typeof(cl) <: Function, fieldnames(typeof(cl)), cl.a, isbits(cl)
```

```text
(true, (:a,), 3, true)
```

The closure holds `a` as a field, and since `a` is an `Int` the whole closure is `isbits`: it lives in registers or on the stack, and passing it to a function that calls it specializes that function on the exact closure type, which lets the body inline. There is no indirect call unless specialization is defeated.

Two closures from the same source location share a type; two from different locations never do:

```julia
mk(a) = x -> a * x
typeof(mk(3)) === typeof(mk(4)), typeof(x -> x) === typeof(x -> x)
```

```text
(true, false)
```

Consequences:

- A `Vector` of closures from different places is a `Vector{Function}` or `Vector{Any}`, and calling through it is dynamic. If you need many interchangeable callbacks with one concrete type, use a named callable struct, `Base.Fix2`, or FunctionWrappers.jl.
- A closure's field types follow the captured variables. Capturing a variable whose type the compiler cannot pin (reassigned, or a non-`const` global) makes that field `Core.Box` or `Any`.
- The method is compiled once per closure *type*, not per instance. Creating a million closures from one `x -> a * x` costs nothing extra in compilation.
- Capturing large data captures a reference, not a copy; the closure is as cheap as the struct it is.

The mental model that works: an anonymous function is sugar for defining a `struct` with the captured variables as fields plus a call method. That is exactly what happens.
A closure in my hot loop allocates on every call and I can't see why from the code. How do I track it down in the session?

Two checks, in order; each is one `julia_eval_code` call in your existing session.

1. Look for a boxed capture:

```julia
# partial
using InteractiveUtils
@code_warntype make_closure(args...)        # the function that *creates* the closure
```

Search the output for `Core.Box`. A captured variable that is assigned more than once, or assigned after the closure is created, is stored in a box with an `Any` slot; every read or write of it allocates. Fix with `let var = var` around the closure for a captured value, or a `Ref` for a captured counter.

2. If there is no `Core.Box`, check what the closure's call infers:

```julia
# partial
cl = make_closure(args...)
Base.return_types(cl, (ArgType,))
```

`Any` or an abstract type here means the body is unstable: usually a captured non-`const` global, a captured variable of abstract type (an element of a `Vector{Any}`), or a captured `Dict{String,Any}` lookup.

3. For the exact allocating line, use `julia_profile_code` with `kind="alloc"` on a call that runs the loop a few thousand times; evaluate it once through `julia_eval_code` first so compilation does not dominate the samples.

Also check the loop itself: if the closure is stored in a struct field or vector typed `Function` or `Any`, every call is a dynamic dispatch that boxes the return value even when the closure is perfectly stable. In that case the fix is the container's type (parametric field, `FunctionWrapper`), not the closure.
Step 1 shows `total::Core.Box` and the closure is `() -> total` where `total` is accumulated in a loop above it.

That is the read-after-reassignment case. `total` is assigned on every loop iteration and read by a closure created after the loop, so the compiler cannot treat the capture as a value and boxes it.

Capture a single-assignment copy:

```julia
# partial
report = let total = total
    () -> total
end
```

The `let` introduces a new `total` that is assigned exactly once, and the closure captures that one. Re-run `@code_warntype` through `julia_eval_code`: the `Core.Box` should be gone and `Base.return_types(report)` should be `Float64` (or whatever `total` is).

If the closure needs the *live* value of `total` as the loop continues (it is called inside the loop and must see updates), use `total = Ref(0.0)` and `total[] += x`; then the capture is a `Ref{Float64}`, assigned once, and the closure reads `total[]` with no box.

Review this struct from a package I'm maintaining:

```julia
mutable struct Simulation
    step!::Function
    observer::Function
    state::Vector{Float64}
end

function run!(sim::Simulation, n)
    for _ in 1:n
        sim.step!(sim.state)
        sim.observer(sim.state)
    end
    sim
end
```

Profiling shows `run!` allocating on every iteration even though `step!` and `observer` don't.

The fields typed `Function` are the problem. `Function` is abstract, so each `sim.step!(...)` is a dynamic dispatch and the return value of the call is boxed. The closures themselves are fine; the container erases their types.

Make the struct parametric so each field is the concrete type of the function stored in it:

```julia

    step!::S
    observer::O
    state::Vector{Float64}
end

    for _ in 1:n
        sim.step!(sim.state)
        sim.observer(sim.state)
    end
    sim
end

sim = Simulation(x -> (x .*= 0.5; nothing), Returns(nothing), ones(4))
run!(sim, 1)
@allocated(run!(sim, 1000))
```

```text
0
```

`Simulation(f, g, state)` infers `S` and `O` from the arguments, so `run!` is compiled per combination of step and observer and both calls inline or are direct.

Other notes:

- `Returns(nothing)` is a good default observer: concrete type, no allocation, prints clearly.
- Do not annotate the parameters as `S <: Function`; a user's callable struct that is not a `Function` subtype would be rejected for no benefit.
- If the package needs to *swap* `step!` at runtime on the same object, the parametric type cannot change. Then either create a new `Simulation` (cheap; the state vector is shared by reference) or use FunctionWrappers.jl to store a fixed-signature wrapper with a concrete type.
- `mutable struct` is only needed if fields are reassigned; the `state` vector is mutated in place either way, so an immutable `struct` works unless you reassign `sim.state`.

This is the struct-field half of a general rule: argument types in signatures should be wide, field types in structs should be concrete.
What is `mapreduce` and when is it better than `sum(map(f, v))` or a loop?

`mapreduce(f, op, itr)` applies `f` to each element and combines the results with `op`, without materializing the mapped collection. `sum(f, v)`, `maximum(f, v)`, `count(f, v)`, `any(f, v)` and friends are special cases with specialized implementations.

```julia
mapreduce(x -> x^2, +, 1:4), mapreduce(abs, max, [-3, 2]; init=0)
```

```text
(30, 3)
```

Against `sum(map(f, v))`: same result, but `map` allocates the intermediate array. On a 1,000-element vector, `sum(abs2, v)` allocated 0 bytes and `sum(abs2.(v))` allocated about 8 KB on 1.13.2.

Against a hand-written loop: for `+`, `max`, `min` and a few others on arrays, Base's reductions vectorize and, for floating-point `sum`, use pairwise summation for better accuracy. A loop with a branch (`a > r && (r = a)`) typically does not vectorize. Prefer the reduction unless profiling shows otherwise.

Points to remember:

- `init` is required when the collection may be empty, and it sets the accumulator type: `mapreduce(abs, max, Int[]; init=0)` is `0`. Use `zero(T)` for the element type rather than a literal in generic code.
- `mapreduce` does not promise an evaluation order; use `mapfoldl` or `mapfoldr` when `op` is not associative.
- With several collections, `mapreduce(f, op, a, b)` zips them: `mapreduce(*, +, a, b)` is a dot product with no temporary.
- For a reduction that also needs the index, `pairs` or `enumerate` as the iterator and a tuple-valued `f` works, but a loop is usually clearer there.

When a loop is better: an early exit that is not `any`/`all`/`findfirst`, several accumulators updated together, or an accumulator that is not a simple value (building a `Dict`, for instance). Those are loops; forcing them into `mapreduce` costs clarity for no speed.

In my agent session I passed a closure to a library function and the result is slower than calling the library function with a named function. How do I check whether the library specialized on my closure?

Ask the method table which specializations exist, in one `julia_eval_code` call after you have called the function once with your closure:

```julia
# partial
m = only(methods(LibraryModule.the_function))     # or pick the right method from methods(...)
[mi.specTypes for mi in Base.specializations(m)]
```

Read the tuple types:

- An entry like `Tuple{typeof(the_function), var"#23#24", Vector{Float64}}` with your closure's type in the function slot means it specialized; look elsewhere for the slowdown.
- An entry with `Function` (or `Any`) in that slot means the library compiled one generic version for every callback. That happens when the function argument is only passed through to another call and the signature does not use a type parameter (`f::F where {F}`), and it costs a dynamic dispatch plus a boxed return value per call.

If it did not specialize, your options from the outside are limited:

1. Check whether the closure is the actual cost. Compare `@allocated` (via `julia_eval_code`, after a warm-up call) between the closure and a named function; if both allocate, the library's signature is the problem and the fix belongs upstream (a `::F where {F}` type parameter on that argument).
2. If the callback body is heavy, the dispatch overhead is negligible; stop here.
3. For a hot inner loop you control, wrap the library call in your own function barrier that receives the closure as `f::F where {F}` and does the work with a stable return type.

Named function versus closure makes no difference to this rule: both are concrete types, and `Base.specializations` will show either one if the library specialized at all. What differs is boxing: a closure that captures a reassigned variable carries a `Core.Box`; check that with `@code_warntype` on the function that *creates* the closure before blaming the library.
I rewrote a broadcast expression to avoid temporaries. How do I confirm in the session that it really fused into one loop and allocates nothing?

Two checks, both through `julia_eval_code` in your existing session.

1. See what the expression lowers to:

```julia
# partial
@macroexpand @. z = (a + b) * c
```

One `.=` with everything inside it means one fused loop. A separate assignment `y = a .+ b` on its own line is a separate loop and a separate array; `@macroexpand` makes that visible when the code is hidden behind macros or helper functions.

2. Count allocations inside a function, after a warm-up call:

```julia
a = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]; b = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]; c = [100.0, 200.0, 300.0]; z = similar(a)
update!(z, a, b, c) = (@. z = (a + b) * c; z)
update!(z, a, b, c)                    # compile first
@allocated(update!(z, a, b, c))
```

```text
0
```

Zero means fused and in place. A number equal to one array's size (80 bytes for three `Float64` plus header on 1.13.2) means one temporary; twice that means two.

Pitfalls that produce wrong readings:

- Measuring at top level with non-`const` globals: the globals themselves cause allocation. Always wrap in a function or interpolate into `@btime` with `$`.
- Forgetting the first-call compile: `@allocated` on a cold call includes compilation. Call once, then measure.
- Scalars that are not scalars: a `Ref` or a one-element array on the right-hand side broadcasts as a container, which is fine, but a `Vector` you meant as a scalar gives a shape error or an unintended outer loop.

If step 2 is nonzero while step 1 shows a single `.=`, the allocation is inside a function you are broadcasting (it returns an array or a string), not in the broadcast machinery; `julia_profile_code` with `kind="alloc"` on a loop of calls points at the line.
